Implemented this — `:60` now only parses when it matches one of the 27 real leap seconds (converted to UTC first, so the EST example works), and `:61` always fails, same as any other invalid date.

One tweak on top of what you suggested: instead of hand-typing the list, I'm reading it from `pytz`'s bundled tzdata (`zoneinfo/leapseconds`) — same data, just sourced from a dependency we already have, so it updates whenever `pytz` does instead of us touching it by hand. Happy to switch to a plain hardcoded list if you'd rather keep it simpler.

Good call — updated it. `leap_second` now carries the actual raw value (`60` or `61`) instead of just `True`, so you get full fidelity on what the string said, e.g.:

```
DateData(date_obj=datetime(2016, 12, 31, 23, 59, 59, ...), period='day', locale='en', leap_second=60)
```

`date_obj.second` is still always `59` under the hood (that's a hard `datetime` limitation, not something we can avoid), but now nothing is lost — the exact input value is preserved right next to it.

Hi @AdrianAtZyte  — fix for the leap-second issue (#862 / DC-1319).

Turns out `datetime` can't represent `:60` seconds, even though Python's own `strptime` allows it — so any date with `23:59:60` was quietly returning `None`. I fixed it by just clamping `:60`/`:61` down to `:59` before building the `datetime`.

One commenter on the original issue wanted something stricter — only allow `:60` on dates that actually had a real leap second (there's a fixed historical list). I skipped that for now since it'd mean maintaining and updating that list forever, and the actual bug is just "valid-looking time crashes the parser" — being lenient fixes that with way less overhead.

Good to go with the simple clamp, or would you rather I do the stricter version?

Not quite — there's a real behavior change here, not just a refactor.

The exact part that changes things is in `parse_item`. Before:

```python
if relative_base:
    parser._settings = parser._settings.replace(RELATIVE_BASE=relative_base)
    parsed_item = parser.get_date_data(item)
```

`RELATIVE_BASE` only ever got *set*, never *unset* — and `parser` is the same instance reused for every substring and every candidate split in the text. So once one item set `RELATIVE_BASE`, it just stayed on `parser._settings` for every later, unrelated parse, since there was no `else` branch to reset it back to the base settings.

On top of that, split-recursion (`parse_found_objects`) started each candidate split from `current_parsed = []` — an empty chain — so it had no way to look up the *real* preceding date via `set_relative_base` for that split. Any relative-base chaining it appeared to do was really just inheriting whatever `RELATIVE_BASE` leaked over from a previous, unrelated item.

Example: `search_dates("2014. July 13th July 14th")` resolves to 2014 today, but only by that leak — `"July 13th July 14th"` fails to parse as a whole and falls into split-recursion with an empty chain, so it never actually sees "2014" through the intended mechanism. Swap the order of unrelated date sequences in the text and that same leak could just as easily hand you the wrong year.

The fix makes `parser._settings` always explicit on every parse (reset to base settings when there's no relative base) and seeds split-recursion with the real outer chain instead of an empty one, so chaining works through `set_relative_base` for real.

So nothing *intended* breaks — but inputs that were only resolving correctly by luck now do so deterministically instead 🙂

Sounds good — closing this one. Agreed the turn-of-year default is a separate design decision, and `PREFER_DATES_FROM` already covers the reported case for anyone who needs it.

I'll open a separate PR for the `parser._settings` leak using the approach you outlined (seed the split path with the outer chain, set `RELATIVE_BASE` explicitly on every parse, restore base settings when there is none).

Thanks for the detailed review — all four points check out, confirmed each one directly (double-bump with `PREFER_DATES_FROM=future`, English-only connector list, the whitespace-fallback test locking in a real bug, and the same-month-wrap gap).

I tried reworking the fix into the relative-base chaining logic as you suggested (force `PREFER_DATES_FROM='future'` only when chaining off a date that had no explicit year of its own, so it doesn't fire on cases like "2014. July 13th" where the year is meant to carry forward as context, not as an ordering constraint — and only when the user hasn't already set `PREFER_DATES_FROM`, so it can't double up). That version correctly handles the original issue, the Spanish case, the same-month wrap, and the wide-gap case, without needing any text-position lookups or English-only word list.

However, it surfaces a deeper pre-existing issue: `parser` (a `DateDataParser`) is a single shared, mutable object reused across every substring — and every split-candidate explored for a substring — in `parse_found_objects`/`choose_best_split`. `parser._settings` gets reassigned per item (originally just for `RELATIVE_BASE`), and that reassignment persists across unrelated items and even unrelated candidate splits, since nothing resets it between them.

Concretely: `"2014. July 13th July 14th"` (an existing test, unrelated to this PR) only gets year 2014 for "July 13th"/"July 14th" today because of this leak — not because of the "official" `set_relative_base`/`already_parsed` chaining. When "July 13th July 14th" fails to parse as a whole and falls into the split-recursion path, that recursion builds its own chain from a **fresh, empty list**, so "2014" isn't actually visible to it through the intended mechanism. It only inherits year 2014 because `parser._settings` was still holding `RELATIVE_BASE=2014-...` left over from processing the *previous, unrelated* top-level item. When I made `parse_item` reset `parser._settings` to a clean baseline before each attempt (to stop *our* future-bias override from leaking the same way), that pre-existing test's accidental year-inheritance broke too — it fell back to today's real year.

So there are two separable things here: (1) the double-bump/English-only/whitespace-bug/same-month issues in our current PR, which I can fix; and (2) this shared-mutable-parser-settings leak, which predates our PR and which some existing tests' expectations are quietly depending on.

I'm not sure how to proceed here — do we close this and pursue the two issues separately? Let me know please.
